15:T18f5,<p>AWS keeps inventing policies. S3 bucket policy, SQS queue policy, SNS topic policy, Lambda function policy, KMS key policy, API Gateway resource policy, IAM role policy. It looks like a dozen things to learn.</p>
<p>It's one thing.</p>
<h2>One shape</h2>
<p>Every one of them is this JSON:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="json" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="json" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">{</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">  "Version"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">"2012-10-17"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">  "Statement"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: [{</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">    "Effect"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">"Allow"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,            </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// or Deny</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">    "Principal"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: { },             </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// who</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">    "Action"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: [</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">"s3:GetObject"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">],   </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// what they may do</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">    "Resource"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">"arn:..."</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,        </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// on which thing</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">    "Condition"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: { }              </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// when (optional)</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  }]</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>Learn it once and you can read any AWS policy. The service prefix on the action (<code>s3:</code>, <code>sqs:</code>, <code>kms:</code>) is the only part that really changes.</p>
<h2>The one split that matters</h2>
<p>There are really just two kinds, and <code>Principal</code> ("who") is the tell.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Identity-based policy.</strong> Attached to an IAM user, group, or role. It has <strong>no <code>Principal</code></strong>. The "who" is already settled: it's the identity you stapled the policy to.</li>
<li><strong>Resource-based policy.</strong> Attached to a <em>thing</em>: a bucket, a queue, a key. It <strong>must name a <code>Principal</code></strong>, because the thing has no idea who's knocking until you say so.</li>
</ul>
<p>That's the entire distinction. Put a policy on an identity, drop the Principal. Put it on a resource, name the Principal.</p>
<p>So the dozen names collapse into two piles:</p>













<table><thead><tr><th>Identity-based (no Principal)</th><th>Resource-based (needs Principal)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>IAM user / group / role policy</td><td>S3 bucket, SQS, SNS, Lambda, KMS key, Secrets Manager, API Gateway, VPC endpoint, DynamoDB, ...</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>The resource list keeps growing. When unsure, ask: can I attach a policy directly to this thing? If yes, it's resource-based and wants a Principal.</p>
<h2>Two that break the mold</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>CloudFormation stack policy</strong> is a fake-out. Same-looking JSON, but it isn't about access at all. It guards which resources a stack update is allowed to touch. No Principal, because there's no "who."</li>
<li><strong><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/introducing-resource-control-policies-rcps-a-new-authorization-policy/">RCP (Resource Control Policy)</a></strong>, added late 2024, is the new arrival. It sits at the AWS Organizations level and caps what every resource-based policy in your org is allowed to grant. Same family, bigger blast radius.</li>
</ul>
<h2>S3 is the cautionary tale</h2>
<p>S3 is where this sprawl got out of hand. One bucket can be governed by a bucket policy, your IAM policies, <strong>and</strong> ACLs at the same time, with a Block Public Access switch over the top. Several knobs, one bucket.</p>
<p>The odd one out is the <strong>ACL</strong>. It predates IAM policies and doesn't use the JSON shape at all: no <code>Effect</code>, no <code>Action</code>, no <code>Condition</code>. Just a coarse "grant this account or group READ/WRITE," in its own format. The mechanism that never fit.</p>
<p>That overlap leaked real data: a bucket read private by its policy while an ACL quietly said otherwise. So AWS changed the default. New buckets now ship with <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/about-object-ownership.html">ACLs disabled</a> ("Bucket owner enforced"), and the guidance is to leave them off and use bucket policies alone. The cure for too many shapes was to delete one.</p>
<h2>The takeaway</h2>
<p>Next time AWS hands you a new "X policy," relearn nothing. Ask one question: <strong>does it have a <code>Principal</code>?</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>No, it's identity-based. Attached to a who.</li>
<li>Yes, it's resource-based. Attached to a what, and you're naming the who.</li>
</ul>
<p>One shape, one question. The dozen names were never a dozen things.</p>16:Td95,
AWS keeps inventing policies. S3 bucket policy, SQS queue policy, SNS topic policy, Lambda function policy, KMS key policy, API Gateway resource policy, IAM role policy. It looks like a dozen things to learn.

It's one thing.

## One shape

Every one of them is this JSON:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",            // or Deny
    "Principal": { },             // who
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],   // what they may do
    "Resource": "arn:...",        // on which thing
    "Condition": { }              // when (optional)
  }]
}
```

Learn it once and you can read any AWS policy. The service prefix on the action (`s3:`, `sqs:`, `kms:`) is the only part that really changes.

## The one split that matters

There are really just two kinds, and `Principal` ("who") is the tell.

- **Identity-based policy.** Attached to an IAM user, group, or role. It has **no `Principal`**. The "who" is already settled: it's the identity you stapled the policy to.
- **Resource-based policy.** Attached to a *thing*: a bucket, a queue, a key. It **must name a `Principal`**, because the thing has no idea who's knocking until you say so.

That's the entire distinction. Put a policy on an identity, drop the Principal. Put it on a resource, name the Principal.

So the dozen names collapse into two piles:

| Identity-based (no Principal) | Resource-based (needs Principal) |
|---|---|
| IAM user / group / role policy | S3 bucket, SQS, SNS, Lambda, KMS key, Secrets Manager, API Gateway, VPC endpoint, DynamoDB, ... |

The resource list keeps growing. When unsure, ask: can I attach a policy directly to this thing? If yes, it's resource-based and wants a Principal.

## Two that break the mold

- **CloudFormation stack policy** is a fake-out. Same-looking JSON, but it isn't about access at all. It guards which resources a stack update is allowed to touch. No Principal, because there's no "who."
- **[RCP (Resource Control Policy)](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/introducing-resource-control-policies-rcps-a-new-authorization-policy/)**, added late 2024, is the new arrival. It sits at the AWS Organizations level and caps what every resource-based policy in your org is allowed to grant. Same family, bigger blast radius.

## S3 is the cautionary tale

S3 is where this sprawl got out of hand. One bucket can be governed by a bucket policy, your IAM policies, **and** ACLs at the same time, with a Block Public Access switch over the top. Several knobs, one bucket.

The odd one out is the **ACL**. It predates IAM policies and doesn't use the JSON shape at all: no `Effect`, no `Action`, no `Condition`. Just a coarse "grant this account or group READ/WRITE," in its own format. The mechanism that never fit.

That overlap leaked real data: a bucket read private by its policy while an ACL quietly said otherwise. So AWS changed the default. New buckets now ship with [ACLs disabled](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/about-object-ownership.html) ("Bucket owner enforced"), and the guidance is to leave them off and use bucket policies alone. The cure for too many shapes was to delete one.

## The takeaway

Next time AWS hands you a new "X policy," relearn nothing. Ask one question: **does it have a `Principal`?**

- No, it's identity-based. Attached to a who.
- Yes, it's resource-based. Attached to a what, and you're naming the who.

One shape, one question. The dozen names were never a dozen things.
